lesson.text: Quick memory: is a letter written in 1925 a primary or a secondary source about the 1920s? (Primary: it was written at the time.) Sources like it help us compare life then and now.
About 100 years ago, in the 1920s, many homes had no electricity. People lit oil lamps, gas lamps or candles, and cooked and kept warm with coal or wood fires.
Washing clothes could take a whole day: water was heated, clothes were scrubbed on a washboard and squeezed through a mangle. Many homes had a toilet outside in the yard.
At school, classes were often big, with 40 or more children in rows. Younger children wrote on small slates with chalk; older ones used pens dipped in ink. They chanted their times tables together.
Toys were often made of wood, tin or cloth: spinning tops, hoops, marbles, skipping ropes, rag dolls and teddy bears. There was no television at home, and no computers or video games.
Some things changed a lot, like lights, phones and travel. Some stayed the same: children still skip, play marbles and chasing games, and go to school.
Try it in the world: build a 1920s room with a fire of stone, a lantern for light and a wooden table. Then build a room of today beside it. What changed?

exercises.prompt: About 100 years ago, most children had video games at home.
exercises.hint: Were there computers and screens in homes 100 years ago?
exercises.explain: False: there were no video games then. Children played with tops, hoops, marbles and dolls.

exercises.prompt: What did many homes use for light 100 years ago?
exercises.hint: Many homes had no electricity yet.
choices: oil lamps, gas lamps and candles
exercises.explain: Many homes had no electricity, so they used oil lamps, gas lamps and candles.

exercises.prompt: Which toy did children play with 100 years ago?
exercises.explain: A spinning top: toys were made of wood, tin or cloth. The others need electricity and came much later.

exercises.prompt: Children still play skipping and marbles today.
exercises.explain: True: some games have lasted over 100 years, like skipping, marbles and chasing games.

exercises.prompt: How did young children often write at school 100 years ago?
exercises.hint: Paper cost more then. What could be wiped clean and used again?
exercises.explain: Young children wrote on small slates with chalk, which could be wiped and used again.

exercises.prompt: Washing clothes by hand, with a washboard and a mangle, could take a whole day.
exercises.hint: Think of heating the water, scrubbing, squeezing and drying, with no machine.
exercises.explain: True: with no washing machine, washing day was hard work that often took all day.

exercises.prompt: Put these ways of lighting a home in order, oldest first.
exercises.hint: People had fire in the Stone Age. Electric bulbs needed electricity.
exercises.explain: Fire first (the Stone Age), then candles (thousands of years ago), gas lamps (about 200 years ago), and then electric bulbs.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is the same then and now?
exercises.hint: Three of these changed. Which one still happens today?
choices: clothes are washed on a washboard
exercises.explain: Children went to school then and still do now. The other things changed.

exercises.prompt: Why did washing take so long 100 years ago?
exercises.hint: What machine does the washing in many homes today?
choices: most homes had no washing machine
exercises.explain: Most homes had no washing machine, so everything was done by hand.

exercises.prompt: Television was invented in the 1920s, but almost no homes had one then.
exercises.hint: An invention can take many years to reach most homes.
exercises.explain: True: television was first shown in 1926, but it was years before many homes had one.

exercises.prompt: Which source would best show a classroom of 1925?
exercises.hint: Which one is a primary source, made at the time?
choices: a photo taken in that classroom in 1925
a film made last year about the 1920s
exercises.explain: A photo taken in 1925 is a primary source: it shows the classroom as it really was.

exercises.prompt: Put these toys in order of when they were first made, oldest first.
exercises.hint: Marbles were played in ancient times. Which toys need electricity?
exercises.explain: Marbles (thousands of years ago), the teddy bear (about 1902), video games (the 1970s), tablets (the 2000s).

exercises.prompt: Over 100 years, some things change a lot and some stay the same.
exercises.hint: Compare lights and toys with going to school.
exercises.explain: True: lights, phones and toys changed a lot, while school and playground games stayed.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: 100 years ago, or today?
exercises.hint: Which ones need electricity? Many homes had none 100 years ago.
exercises.explain: 100 years ago: slate and chalk, oil lamp, washboard. Today: tablet, electric light, washing machine.

exercises.prompt: Sort the jobs at home: how they were done 100 years ago, or today?
exercises.hint: Did it need electricity, or was it done by hand with fire and lamps?
exercises.explain: 100 years ago: washboards, oil lamps and coal fires, done by hand. Today: washing machines, electric lights and central heating.

exercises.prompt: Match each thing from 1925 to what does its job today.
exercises.hint: Think what each one was for, then what does that job now.
exercises.explain: Slates gave way to paper, pencils and later tablets. Oil lamps gave way to electric lights. Washboards gave way to washing machines. Many letters are now emails or messages.

exercises.prompt: The first teddy bears were made about 1902. The first home video games came about 1972. About how many years apart is that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
exercises.explain: 1972 − 1902 = 70 years. Both are new compared with marbles, which children have played with for thousands of years.
